script.text: Many of us dread losing an hour of sleep as we spring forward an hour once a year. Some of us relish gaining an hour of sleep as we fall back. Some of us enjoy the time change to make use of the extra sunlight in the summer, but is that really worth the disruption it causes?
script.label: Intro captions 1

script.text:
Since 2018, Congress has introduced five versions of legislation to end the seasonal time change, each called the Sunshine Protection Act. The 2021 version passed the Senate, and the current version passed the House on July 14, 2026 and is now under consideration in the Senate.

It keeps Daylight Saving Time year-round for most of the United States.

So should we pass it?
script.label: Intro captions 2

script.text:
To answer that, we need to investigate the health, economic, debt and other impacts to determine if the bill would produce a net benefit for the country.

Reason Tracker is a video series where you help map out all the reasons for and against controversial decisions.
script.label: Intro captions 3

script.text:
Each decision is explored across several videos that compare both sides, make support and uncertainty explicit, and improve over time as you contribute feedback and new evidence.

As we go, if you notice missing claims, reasons, or piece of evidence, tell us. Useful additions can change the map in later videos.
script.label: Intro captions 4

mainClaim.text: The United States would experience a net benefit from enacting the Sunshine Protection Act of 2025 [H.R. 139], to establish permanent Daylight Saving Time.

script.text: We start with the main claim of "The United States would experience a net benefit from enacting the Sunshine Protection Act of 2025, to establish permanent Daylight Saving Time." To understand how each piece of information changes we use a simple predictable formula that just takes into account what has been explicitly added so far. It starts at 100%.
script.label: Formula intro 1

script.text: That does not mean Reason Tracker thinks we should pass the bill. It means we have not added anything yet that reduces the case for it.
script.label: Formula intro 2

script.text: The Reason Tracker formula scores based solely on what has been entered. Missing information does not count against either side.
script.label: Formula intro 3

script.text:
So as you tell us reasons, evidence, rebuttals, weight the score will change using the same predictable formula each time.

Think of 100% as our starting point, not our conclusion.
script.label: Formula intro 4

script.text: This legislation would have a substantial cost.
script.label: Add substantial cost

script.text: Let's add the claim that this legislation would have a substantial cost.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: With only that claim added, the score drops to 0%.
script.label: Narration

script.text: But remember, all we have so far is one reason not to do it. Let's keep adding information and see how the score changes.
script.label: Narration

script.text: It might improve use of daylight.
script.label: Add useful evening daylight

script.text: Next, it might improve use of daylight.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: With one claim for it and one claim against it, the score goes up to 50%.
script.label: Narration

script.text: Let's look at health and safety next.
script.label: Narration

script.text: Ending seasonal clock changes would improve acute health and safety on balance.
script.label: Add acute health and safety

script.text: Ending the seasonal clock changes would improve acute health and safety on balance. The twice-yearly clock changes disrupt sleep schedules, and the spring change has also been associated with cardiovascular events, motor-vehicle crashes, injuries, and workplace accidents.
script.label: Health and safety summary

script.text: Add that as one health-and-safety reason for the bill, and the score moves to about 67%.
script.label: Narration

script.text: But this bill does more than end the clock changes. It specifically chooses permanent Daylight Saving Time.
script.label: Narration

script.text: Permanent Daylight Saving Time would worsen circadian alignment, sleep, and related health or performance outcomes on balance.
script.label: Add chronic circadian risk

script.text: That might worsen circadian alignment and sleep because winter mornings would stay darker and evening light would come later.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: Add that, and the score comes back to 50%.
script.label: Narration

script.text: This distinction matters. There can be good reasons to stop changing the clocks without those reasons automatically being good reasons for permanent Daylight Saving Time.
script.label: Narration

script.text: From here, we'll keep the score visible, but we don't need to read every change out loud.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: Permanent Daylight Saving Time would improve physical-activity and recreation opportunities on balance.
script.label: Add physical activity evidence

script.text: More evening daylight might make exercise, recreation, and after-school activities easier. There is evidence that evening daylight can increase children's physical activity, and it can be especially useful for people whose free time is mostly after work or school.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: Permanent Daylight Saving Time would benefit consumer activity and affected businesses on balance.
script.label: Add economic and business benefit

script.text: It could also help some businesses. More evening light may increase shopping, dining, tourism, golf, and other activity that happens after work.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: Evidence for a large national economic boost from permanent Daylight Saving Time is weak.
script.label: Add economic rebuttal

script.text: But there is a rebuttal to the broader economic claim. The evidence that permanent Daylight Saving Time would create a large national economic boost is weak.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: Notice what happens here. We do not count that as a completely separate reason against the bill. It directly weakens the claim that the bill would create a large economic benefit.
script.label: Narration

script.text: Permanent Daylight Saving Time would improve road and travel safety on balance.
script.label: Add road safety

script.text: Road safety is also mixed.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: Permanent Daylight Saving Time may reduce overall fatal crashes by aligning daylight with higher-traffic evening periods.
script.label: Add road-safety support

script.text: Shifting daylight later could reduce pedestrian and bicyclist fatalities because more travel happens in the evening than in the morning.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: A systematic review found the road-safety evidence insufficient to support or refute a net benefit from permanently shifting daylight from morning to evening.
script.label: Add road-safety rebuttal

script.text: But some recent evidence points toward more motor-vehicle occupant fatalities, and a systematic review found the overall road-safety evidence insufficient to say that permanently shifting daylight later produces a net benefit.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: Health has a similar complication.
script.label: Narration

script.text: A large English cohort study found little evidence that the spring clock change increases several acute mental and physical health events.
script.label: Add acute-health evidence limitation

script.text: There is evidence that the spring clock change causes short-term disruption, but some large recent studies did not find increases in several of the acute health outcomes that are often blamed on the change.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: At the same time, the concern about permanent Daylight Saving Time is not just the one-hour transition. It is the possibility of chronic circadian misalignment from later winter morning light.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: A broad set of medical, sleep, safety, and parent organizations endorse permanent Standard Time rather than permanent Daylight Saving Time.
script.label: Add medical consensus

script.text: A broad set of medical and sleep organizations favors permanent Standard Time instead.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: A recent circadian model projected that either permanent Standard Time or permanent Daylight Saving Time would reduce circadian burden compared with biannual clock switching.
script.label: Add circadian model counterpoint

script.text: There is also a recent model suggesting either permanent clock could reduce some circadian burden compared with switching twice a year, although that model favored Standard Time on some health outcomes and has itself been challenged on methodology.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: So the health branch is not simply "changing clocks is bad, therefore permanent Daylight Saving Time is good."
script.label: Script caption

script.text: There are also implementation costs.
script.label: Narration

script.text: A permanent change could create temporary scheduling and coordination problems for airlines, schools, workplaces, transit systems, and international travel. Advance notice can reduce some of that disruption.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: The bill also limits future flexibility. States that currently observe seasonal Daylight Saving Time would not be able to switch to permanent Standard Time on their own later without another change in federal law.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: Permanent Daylight Saving Time would be broadly acceptable to the public on balance.
script.label: Add public preference

script.text: Public preference is mixed too.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: Historical experiences with permanent Daylight Saving Time or permanent summer time are unfavorable on balance.
script.label: Add historical evidence

script.text: We also have historical evidence.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: The United States tried year-round Daylight Saving Time in 1974. It became unpopular, largely because of dark winter mornings.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: Russia adopted permanent summer time in 2011 and reversed it in 2014 after similar complaints.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: The 1974 U.S. experience may be a weaker guide today because school and commuting patterns have changed.
script.label: Add historical limitation

script.text: Those examples count against the bill, but they are not perfect experiments. School schedules, commuting patterns, lighting, and other conditions have changed, so we should not treat them as automatic proof of what would happen now.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: Nineteen states have enacted laws or trigger provisions supporting year-round Daylight Saving Time if federal law permits it.
script.label: Add state support

script.text: Some polls show strong support for permanent Daylight Saving Time, and nineteen states have passed laws or trigger provisions supporting it if federal law allows it.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: A 2025 Gallup poll found that permanent Standard Time was preferred substantially more often than permanent Daylight Saving Time when respondents were offered permanent Standard Time, permanent Daylight Saving Time, or seasonal switching.
script.label: Add Gallup preference rebuttal

script.text: But a 2025 Gallup poll that gave people three choices found permanent Standard Time was preferred substantially more often than permanent Daylight Saving Time.
script.label: Script caption

script.text: Ending seasonal clock changes would reduce recurring household and schedule disruption on balance.
script.label: Add schedule convenience

script.text: The Sunshine Protection Act would improve energy and emissions outcomes on balance.
script.label: Add energy and emissions

script.text: Permanent Daylight Saving Time would improve crime-related public safety on balance.
script.label: Add crime-related safety

script.text: The Sunshine Protection Act would worsen outcomes for agriculture and other sun-tied work on balance.
script.label: Add sun-tied work costs

script.text: Permanent Daylight Saving Time would harm AM broadcasting and the services it provides on balance.
script.label: Add AM broadcasting costs

script.text: Permanent Daylight Saving Time would push sunrise-based Orthodox Jewish morning prayer times later, creating conflicts with work or school schedules.
script.label: Add religious schedule costs

script.text: There are some obvious pros and cons to this that we do not have time to cover one by one here: energy use, crime, deer collisions, agriculture and other sun-tied work, AM radio, religious schedules, household routines, and the simple annoyance of changing clocks twice a year.
script.label: Other pros and cons

script.text: Modern electricity savings from Daylight Saving Time may be negligible.
script.label: Rebut energy savings

script.text: Added evening daylight reduces robberies.
script.label: Add robbery reduction

script.text: Added evening daylight can increase aggravated assaults around sunset by increasing foot traffic or social interaction.
script.label: Rebut the crime benefit

script.text: Year-round Daylight Saving Time would reduce deer-vehicle collisions and associated human, wildlife, and economic costs.
script.label: Add deer-collision effects

script.text: Those claims are in the map too. In later videos we can go deeper into the strongest ones, the weakest ones, and the places where the evidence conflicts.
script.label: Closing narration

script.text: The score on screen is not a final verdict. It is just what follows from the claims, rebuttals, and relationships we have entered so far.
script.label: Closing narration
